title: NHC storm surge ranges in Atlantic advisories (47 US storms, 2017-2025) were exceeded at 10% of tide gauges, mostly by about 0.8 ft of background sea level that the ranges appear to omit
abstract: We tested the storm surge ranges in NHC Atlantic public advisories ('the water could reach X-Y ft above ground somewhere in the indicated areas if the peak surge occurs at the time of high tide') against NOAA tide gauges. We parsed 5,695 advisories from 2017 to 2025 (1,315 with surge lists, 6,488 US range items), matched segments to 125 CO-OPS gauges, and used peak 6-minute water level above MHHW. The plan was written before we downloaded water levels. For the last advisory issued 6 h or more before the gauge peak (810 storm-gauge units, 47 storms), the peak was below the range in 36% (storm bootstrap 95% interval 28-45%), inside it in 54% and above it in 9.8% (5.7-13.6%). First advisories (median 53 h before the peak) gave the same result, so early track and intensity errors did not cause the misses. When we moved the observed peak surge to high tide, as the text assumes, 21% (16-27%) were above. The ranges were too sharp: the peak rose 0.30 ft per 1 ft of range midpoint; ranges with an upper end above 6 ft were below at 85% of gauges. Exceedances came mostly from weak, broad Gulf storms and gauges more than 150 km right of the track. In exploratory analyses, monthly mean sea level at storm time was a median 0.80 ft above the tidal-epoch mean sea level (0.56 ft relative sea-level rise since 1983-2001 plus 0.24 ft seasonal high water). Without this background, 1.5% (0.4-2.9%) of units were above the range, and 5.4% with the high-tide condition. The gauge error rose with the background at a slope of 0.83 (0.37-1.31), near the slope of 1 expected if the ranges omit it; both its parts gave similar slopes. Results held in nine sensitivity runs (above 6.4-12.8%). Limitations: one gauge cannot measure the segment maximum; USGS high-water marks were not available; MHHW is only a proxy for ground; river gauges include rain runoff; the background regression is observational; only active gauges were used.
